question: Which sentence correctly explains the purpose of an action?

options.label: A) Companies hold weekly meetings to help remote teams stay connected.
B) Companies hold weekly meetings for help remote teams stay connected.
C) Companies hold weekly meetings to helping remote teams stay connected.

successMsg: Correct! In English, use 'to + base verb' (to help) to explain why you do something.
errorMsg: Not quite. Use 'to + base verb' ('to help') to show purpose, not 'for + verb' or 'to + -ing'.

question: Choose the sentence where the verb matches the subject correctly:

options.label: A) Many students uses online tools to practice their English.
B) Many students use online tools to practice their English.
C) Many student use online tools to practice their English.

successMsg: Great job! 'Many students' is plural, so it takes the base verb 'use' without '-s'.
errorMsg: Check the plural subject 'Many students'. Plural subjects take 'use', not 'uses'.

question: Which sentence uses the adverb correctly to describe a verb?

options.label: A) Technology is changing our daily lives very quick.
B) Technology is changing our daily lives quickly.
C) Technology is quick changing our daily lives.

successMsg: Well done! Adverbs ending in '-ly' (like 'quickly') describe how an action happens.
errorMsg: Remember to use the adverb 'quickly' (not the adjective 'quick') to describe the verb 'changing'.

question: Which sentence uses a contrast connector correctly?

options.label: A) Working from home saves time. However, it can feel lonely.
B) Working from home saves time. Because, it can feel lonely.
C) Working from home saves time. Furthermore, it can feel lonely.

successMsg: Correct! 'However' clearly introduces a contrasting or opposite idea.
errorMsg: 'However' is used to show contrast between a positive point and a negative point.

question: Choose the sentence that uses 'affect' or 'effect' correctly:

options.label: A) Poor sleep can effect your focus at work.
B) Poor sleep can affect your focus at work.
C) Poor sleep has a strong affect on your focus at work.

successMsg: Nice! 'Affect' is usually the action verb ('can affect'), while 'effect' is usually a noun ('has an effect').
errorMsg: Use 'affect' as the verb ('can affect') and 'effect' as the noun ('a strong effect').

question: Which sentence correctly describes a finished action at a specific past time?

options.label: A) I have visited Madrid two years ago.
B) I visited Madrid two years ago.
C) I was visit Madrid two years ago.

successMsg: Correct! With finished time markers like 'two years ago', always use the past simple ('visited').
errorMsg: Do not use present perfect ('have visited') with a specific finished time like 'two years ago'.

question: Choose the sentence with the correct time prepositions:

options.label: A) Our English class starts at 9:00 a.m. on Mondays.
B) Our English class starts on 9:00 a.m. in Mondays.
C) Our English class starts in 9:00 a.m. at Mondays.

successMsg: Well done! Use 'at' for exact clock times and 'on' for days of the week.
errorMsg: Remember: 'at' is used for clock times ('at 9:00 a.m.') and 'on' is used for days ('on Mondays').

question: Which sentence uses a modal verb with the correct verb form?

options.label: A) You should to read a few pages in English every night.
B) You should reading a few pages in English every night.
C) You should read a few pages in English every night.

successMsg: Correct! Modal verbs like 'should', 'can', and 'must' are always followed by the base verb without 'to'.
errorMsg: After modal verbs like 'should', use the base verb directly ('should read'), never 'to + verb' or '-ing'.

question: Which sentence handles the uncountable noun 'advice' or 'information' properly?

options.label: A) She gave me some useful advice before my interview.
B) She gave me many useful advices before my interview.
C) She gave me an useful advice before my interview.

successMsg: Spot on! 'Advice' is uncountable in English, so we use 'some advice' or 'a piece of advice', never 'advices'.
errorMsg: 'Advice' is uncountable in English, so it has no plural '-s' and cannot take 'a/an' or 'many'.

question: Choose the grammatically correct sentence:

options.label: A) I am looking forward to meet your team tomorrow.
B) I am looking forward to meeting your team tomorrow.
C) I am looking forward for meeting your team tomorrow.

successMsg: Great! In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by the '-ing' form ('meeting').
errorMsg: 'Look forward to' takes a gerund ('-ing' form), so 'looking forward to meeting' is the natural form.

question: Which sentence forms the comparative adjective correctly?

options.label: A) Cycling to work is more healthier than driving.
B) Cycling to work is healthyer than driving.
C) Cycling to work is healthier than driving.

successMsg: Correct! For two-syllable adjectives ending in '-y', change '-y' to '-ier' ('healthier') without adding 'more'.

question: Which sentence uses 'make' or 'do' naturally?

options.label: A) Everyone makes mistakes when learning a new language.
B) Everyone does mistakes when learning a new language.
C) Everyone takes mistakes when learning a new language.

successMsg: Nice! In English, the natural collocation is always 'make a mistake', never 'do a mistake'.

question: Choose the sentence that uses the first conditional accurately:

options.label: A) If it will rain tomorrow, we will stay inside.
B) If it rains tomorrow, we will stay inside.
C) If it rained tomorrow, we will stay inside.

successMsg: Correct! In a first conditional, use the present simple in the 'if' clause ('If it rains') and 'will' in the main clause.
errorMsg: Do not put 'will' inside the 'if' clause for real future conditions; use present simple ('If it rains').

question: Which sentence uses the relative pronoun correctly?

options.label: A) The book who I borrowed from the library was fascinating.
B) The book what I borrowed from the library was fascinating.
C) The book that I borrowed from the library was fascinating.

successMsg: Well done! Use 'that' or 'which' for things like 'the book', and 'who' for people.
errorMsg: Use 'that' or 'which' for objects/things ('the book'), not 'who' or 'what'.

question: Which sentence clearly connects a reason with its result?

options.label: A) Traffic was heavy, so I arrived ten minutes late.
B) Because traffic was heavy, so I arrived ten minutes late.
C) Traffic was heavy, although I arrived ten minutes late.

successMsg: Correct! Use either 'so' OR 'because' to connect cause and result—never both in the same sentence.
errorMsg: In English, do not use both 'because' and 'so' together; use one connector between the two clauses.
